title: The 1,600-Year-Old Indian Iron Pillar That Never Rusts
sources: R. Balasubramaniam (IIT Kanpur) 'Delhi Iron Pillar: New Insights' - Metallurgical analysis of the 4th-century Gupta Empire pillar showing high-phosphorus misawite protective film.
Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) - The 6,000 kg forged iron pillar at the Qutb complex in Delhi has resisted rust for 1,600 years of monsoon climate.

lines.text: In New Delhi, India stands a massive six-ton ancient iron pillar -
lines.caps: In New Delhi, India | stands a 6-ton iron pillar | that has survived 1,600 years - | WITHOUT RUSTING!

lines.text: that has survived sixteen hundred years of scorching heat and monsoon rains without a single spot of rust.
Forged in the fourth century during the golden age of the Gupta Empire, it stands over twenty-three feet tall.
Under normal conditions, iron left outdoors oxidizes and dissolves into orange rust within a few years.
Yet this ancient Indian monument has stood under Delhi's open skies for over sixteen centuries,
looking as solid as the day it was forged.
When top scientists from IIT Kanpur analyzed the metal under advanced electron microscopes, they were stunned.
Ancient Indian metallurgists had invented an advanced forge-welding technique with high phosphorus content.
It created a microscopic self-healing film of iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate called misawite across the metal surface.
Whenever moisture touches the pillar, the ancient coating repairs itself, making it completely rustproof!
A metallurgical miracle of ancient Indian engineering that modern science is still trying to replicate today.
